newsitem.title: USA: European bourse executives battle for EMU business.
newsitem.headline: European bourse executives battle for EMU business.

text.p: Top executives from four of Europe's largest futures and options exchanges engaged in a public skirmish in Chicago on Thursday, using an industry conference to debate which bourse will become the dominant derivatives centre in Europe after monetary union.
The tone began with remarks by Daniel Hodson, chief executive of the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), and grew gradually more heated.
"The people you see sitting at this table are, first of all, great friends," Hodson said. "(But) we are involved in a battle. The battle of the EMU has just begun."

Hodson argued that London is and will remain the dominant futures and options market in Europe, regardless of whether EMU occurs and whether Britain is part of it. That assertion drew a quick response from co-panelists.
"As Daniel said, we were good friends," Gerard Pfauwadel, president and general director of MATIF SA, said to shouts of laughter. "I do not agree at all with what you have to say, Daniel," he added.
Pfauwadel said that Britain, as a financial center outside the EMU, might have "some advantages" but maintained that Paris would be the "real" center of activity.
"I do consider Paris will be the gateway to Europe," he said, replacing the word "London" with "Paris" in an assertion made earlier by Hodson.

Pfaudwadel cited two reasons for this: timing and critical mass. Paris will have an advantage over London because it will be part of EMU in 1999. Stock, fixed income and foreign exchange markets in France will instantly convert to the euro, which will create instant liquidity, he said, calling this MATIF's trump in the redistribution of cards.
"I am absolutely convinced that...the fact that you do not have unlimited access to the liquidity of the intra-day central bank money is a deep problem," he said.
Jack Wigglesworth, chairman of LIFFE, speaking from audience, called this argument a "red herring." London already does substantial business in derivatives on the German mark, he said.

"London has always thrived from other people's restrictive practices," he remarked. "London is not connected as a financial services center to the fortunes of the British economy, or any decision as to which currencies are going to be in or out of this attempt to create an unprecedented single currency amongst massive countries that are all different."
However, Jose-Luis Oller, general manager and chief executive of the Spanish Financial Futures and Options Exchange (MEFF), also discounted LIFFE's position.
"The first thing you do in a battle is you try to frighten your adversaries to death and this is exactly what Daniel has done, without success," he said of Hodson's remarks.
Oller said his exchange plans to concentrate on maintaining domestic business, which accounts for 75 percent of its total, rather than worrying about the 25 percent it might lose.

Joerg Franke, general manager and member of the executive board of Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB), struck a more conciliatory note after initially echoing Pfaudwadel's questioning of Hodson's statistics.
"We have some nice figures as well," he said, calling DTB the largest derivatives market in Europe "although London is bigger for stocks."
That comment contradicted Hodson's assertion that LIFFE is the largest center outside Chicago for exchange-traded derivatives.
However, Franke said he regretted there was not greater cooperation among the exchanges.
Pfaudwadel showed fewer regrets.
"It is true in the long run we may have to again consider cooperation," he said. "But first we have to have the battle of the fill."
